relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused (sharesOptionSetWith) - repurposed from its original DurabilityLevel-enum-scope-sharing use to a timeout-value inheritance fact; same shape ('the same configured value applies at two structurally distinct scopes')
relations.evidence: Timers follow the same timeout semantics as their Parent Functions. So, if an Eventing Function has an execution timeout of 60 seconds, each of the timers created from the Eventing Function inherits the same execution timeout value of 60 seconds.

relations.evidence: The Eventing Storage (or Metadata) collection stores information about timers and its association with an Eventing Function's handler.

relations.subject: eventing:function

notable_absence.finding: No access-control or edition content on this page at all - Timers are documented purely as a runtime/language construct with operational caveats (sharding, wall-clock inaccuracy, space budgeting). This is consistent with eventing-rbac.md's finding that access control is gated at the keyspace/Function level, not per-construct; Timers inherit whatever privilege gate applies to the Eventing Storage keyspace they're stored in, with no separate Timer-specific privilege documented anywhere in this batch.

cross_component_finding: Timers are the clearest single confirmation of this batch's hypothesis answer: rather than introducing a new concurrency/scheduling primitive family, Timers are explicitly framed as 'limited asynchrony' bolted onto the existing Function/handler/binding vocabulary - they share the parent Function's timeout setting (sharesOptionSetWith), are stored in the same Eventing Storage keyspace as everything else, reuse the same bucket-alias bindings, and are deleted by the same lifecycle cascade as any other Function-owned resource. No standalone Timer namespace beyond eventing:timer/eventing:timer-callback-handler was needed - it is a controlled variant of the Function/handler pattern, not a parallel structural layer.
